questions.stem: You are examining Josh, 23, in a GP clinic. He has jaundice from acute hepatitis and you want to check for the hepatic flap (asterixis), a sign of encephalopathy and possible acute liver failure. How should you elicit it?
options: Ask him to squeeze two of your fingers firmly in each hand for 10 seconds
Ask him to hold his arms out, palms up and eyes closed, for 20 seconds, noting any drift
Ask him to hold his arms out, wrists cocked back and fingers spread, for 15 seconds
Ask him to touch your finger, then his nose, repeatedly with each hand
questions.why: Asterixis is a failure to hold a posture. With the arms outstretched, wrists dorsiflexed and fingers spread for about 15 seconds, it shows as irregular flapping. Finding it would mean encephalopathy, which needs hospital assessment for acute liver failure.
notes: A sustained grip that waxes and wanes (milkmaid grip) is a sign of chorea, not hepatic encephalopathy.
Holding the arms out with palms up and eyes closed tests for pronator drift, a sign of an upper motor neuron lesion.
Finger-nose testing looks for cerebellar signs (dysmetria and intention tremor), not the flap of metabolic encephalopathy.

questions.stem: Josh, 23, has confirmed acute hepatitis A. His jaundice began 2 days ago. He shares a kitchen and bathroom with three healthy housemates aged 22 to 24. None has liver disease or immunosuppression, and none has been vaccinated against hepatitis A. What should the housemates be offered?
options: One dose of hepatitis A vaccine as soon as possible, ideally within 2 weeks of exposure
Normal human immunoglobulin intramuscularly as soon as possible, instead of vaccine
Two vaccine doses a month apart, started only once serology confirms they are non-immune
No prophylaxis: advise hand hygiene and review only if they develop symptoms
questions.why: Under the Australian Immunisation Handbook, healthy household and sexual contacts aged 12 months or more get hepatitis A vaccine as post-exposure prophylaxis, ideally within 2 weeks of exposure. Normal human immunoglobulin is kept for infants under 12 months, people who are immunocompromised and people with chronic liver disease.
notes: Normal human immunoglobulin is for contacts under 12 months old, immunocompromised contacts or those with chronic liver disease; healthy young adults get the vaccine.
Waiting for serology delays prophylaxis past its 2-week window, and the second dose of hepatitis A vaccine is given 6 to 12 months later, not after a month.
Household contacts sharing a kitchen and bathroom are at real risk, and vaccine given within 2 weeks can prevent infection, so they should be offered it.

questions.stem: Josh, 23, has acute hepatitis A. He is well, with an ALT of 1,240 U/L, an INR of 1.1 and an albumin of 41 g/L. Your GP supervisor says the INR is a better guide than the albumin to how well his liver is coping right now. What best explains this?
options: Albumin is lost in the urine during acute hepatitis, so its level is unreliable
The INR mainly reflects vitamin K absorption, which falls early in any jaundice
Prothrombin is made only by hepatocytes, while albumin is also made in muscle
Factor VII has a half-life of about 6 hours, while albumin's is about 3 weeks
questions.why: The INR depends on liver-made clotting factors, especially factor VII, whose half-life is only a few hours, so it rises within a day or two of synthetic failure. Albumin lasts about 3 weeks, so it stays normal early in acute liver failure and better reflects chronic disease.
notes: Albumin is not lost in the urine in acute hepatitis; urinary loss suggests nephrotic syndrome.
Poor vitamin K absorption matters mainly in long-standing cholestasis with pale stools. Josh's normal INR reflects hepatocyte synthesis, not vitamin K uptake.
Albumin is made only in the liver, not in muscle, so this does not explain why the INR changes sooner.

questions.stem: Josh, 23, has jaundice and a dull right upper quadrant ache. To look for cholecystitis you test for Murphy's sign, placing your fingers over the surface marking of the gallbladder fundus as he breathes in. Where is this?
options: Right mid-clavicular line at the level of the umbilicus, about 8 cm from the midline
Tip of the right 9th costal cartilage, at the lateral border of rectus abdominis
Right 5th intercostal space in the mid-clavicular line, above the costal margin
Midline just below the xiphisternum, over the epigastrium
questions.why: The gallbladder fundus lies at the tip of the right 9th costal cartilage, where the lateral border of rectus abdominis meets the costal margin (near the transpyloric plane). An inflamed gallbladder meets the examining fingers on inspiration, so the breath catches.
notes: The umbilical level in the right mid-clavicular line is well below the gallbladder; palpating here is how you begin feeling for an enlarged liver edge.
The right 5th intercostal space in the mid-clavicular line is about where the upper border of liver dullness lies, not the gallbladder.
The epigastrium overlies the stomach, the left lobe of the liver and the pancreas, not the gallbladder fundus.
